We did not invent him out of an idea. We say he was truly born - of Mary, from the line of David. We say he truly ate and drank. We say he was truly brought before Pilate, truly nailed to the cross, and truly died - not in appearance only, the way some among our own neighbors claimed. And we say he was truly raised, and that we will be raised the same way, by the same Father.

When we give thanks over the cup - the eucharistia, our own word for that thanksgiving - we call it the vine of David his servant, made known to us through Jesus. More than one of our own households uses those words, not only one letter-writer's own. That is the shape of it for us: a real man, really killed, really raised, and now the one through whom we give thanks.

One of us, Ignatius, calls him our God - not once, but often, in how he opens his letters and in how he closes them: “So be on your guard against such people. This will be true for you if you are not puffed up with pride, and if you continue in close union with Jesus Christ our God, with the bishop, and with the apostles' teachings.”

It is worship, not an argument worked out. How calling Jesus God fits together with calling the Father God - with there being one God - none of us whose writing survives ever wrote out. We can tell you plainly that we called him God. We cannot tell you we had settled how.

None of us saw him ourselves. What we have is what was handed to us. The apostles preached what they had received from the Lord; they in turn appointed others to carry it forward when they themselves were gone. In some of our households, on the day we gather, someone reads aloud what the apostles wrote down, for as long as there is time, alongside the words of the prophets before them. That is how it reached us - not by seeing, but by receiving, and by passing on what was received.

We should say this plainly: none of us claims to have known an eyewitness ourselves. Even in our own time, that chain was already felt as something thinning, not something we could simply rely on. What the apostles wrote - their memoirs, their letters - those we read. What was handed on through teaching and through the order of our gathering - that too we received. The path was: Christ to the apostles, the apostles to those they appointed, and those appointed ones to us. But the living voice of someone who walked with him? That was already passing out of reach by the time our own voices begin to speak.

We cannot promise you that belief will come as a sudden thing. Justin, one among us, says he had already gone through other philosophies first, before an old man's words left him with what he calls a flame kindled in his soul. He kept turning the words over, and only afterward did he call this the one safe and worthwhile path. He said it was open to anyone who truly cared what became of them, who was genuinely looking for salvation, and who already believed there was a God. That is Justin's own account - a man with the time and learning to go looking. We do not have the same account from someone without what he had.

What we can tell you is the path we actually walked. Before the water, we taught the Two Ways: a way of life and a way of death lie open before every person, and which one you walk is a choice kept daily. That teaching was given to everyone preparing for baptism, and it treated the choice as real and continuing, not something settled once. The room for doubt was there in the waiting itself - teaching first, then fasting, with someone fasting beside you, before you came to the water. Whether the slowness was meant as kindness to the unsure, our record does not say. But the room for a person still deciding was built into the path.

We would not tell you to force what is not there. Justin himself spent years looking before that flame was kindled: “He said these things, and many others there is no time to mention now. Then he went away, telling me to think them over, and I have not seen him since. But at once a flame was kindled in my soul. A love for the prophets, and for those who are friends of Christ, took hold of me. As I turned his words over in my mind, I found this philosophy alone to be safe and useful. This is why, and this is how, I am a philosopher.”

We can only tell you what we held, and let you weigh it honestly for yourself.

We called Jesus Christ our God - Ignatius does so again and again, in how he opens his letters and in how he closes them. It is not one passing phrase; he reaches for it often. But it is worship, not an argument worked out. How calling Jesus God fits together with calling the Father God - with there being one God - none of us whose writing survives ever wrote out. We can tell you plainly that we called him God. We cannot tell you we had settled how.

We believed in one God, maker of everything. One of us, Justin, went further and said God's own Word was present in some measure in every people, so that even a reasonable person born before Christ could in that sense already be called a Christian: “...and those who lived reasonably are Christians, even though people have thought them atheists. Among the Greeks, such people were Socrates and Heraclitus, and men like them. Among non-Greeks, they were Abraham, Ananias, Azarias, Mishael, Elijah, and many others...”

That is Justin's own reach, not something every one of us argued the same way. What we actually argued about among ourselves, letter after letter, was who should lead us: one bishop - the episkopos - or a council of elders. That was our real fight. No gathering of ours ever met to settle a question about God's nature. That kind of deciding belongs to a later world.

We gathered to give thanks over the bread and cup - the eucharistia, our own word for that thanksgiving. The community returns to this table again and again, to be formed once more into one body. That returning was the shape our worship took. The arguing about God's nature that would come later - the councils, the settled formulas - those had not been invented yet.

We never settled doctrine the way you mean it. No gathering of ours ever met to decide a question about God's own nature. That kind of deciding belongs to a later world. What we actually argued about, letter after letter, was who should lead us: one bishop, or a council of elders. That was our real fight.

Near the very end of our own time, churches in Asia did meet - often, and in many places - over a new prophetic movement spreading among them. But that gathering was about whether to receive a movement. It was not about what God is.

Where disagreement surfaced, it was handled through letters, not councils. Rome wrote to Corinth when Corinth removed some of its own presbyters. The letter that survives is Rome's own argument that those men had served without fault and should be restored. We do not have Corinth's own reasons for what it did, or what became of anyone who still disagreed after the letter arrived.

On what the apostles themselves appointed, one of us put it this way: “For this reason, they appointed the ministers already mentioned. They had full foreknowledge of this. Afterward, they gave instructions: when these men died, other approved men should succeed them in their ministry.”

That is the claim - succession from the apostles' own appointment. But we have to say plainly: the claim and the proof are not the same thing. The claim is ours, made with full confidence. Whether it holds up is a real, open question we cannot close for you, because we cannot close it for ourselves.

We did not hold that. What we taught before the water was not about a nature already settled but about a choice still open. Two ways lie before every person - a way of life and a way of death: “There are two ways: one of life and one of death, and there is a great difference between the two ways. The way of life is this. First, you shall love God, who made you; second, your neighbor as yourself. And all the things you would not want to happen to you, you also must not do to another.”

Which one you walk is a choice kept daily, after the water as much as before it. We never said a child came into the world already guilty. We said a road lay open, and that walking one rather than the other was something you chose, and kept choosing.

We should say plainly: this is how one of our own communities taught it, in a manual we have. We cannot promise you every household among us taught it this same way. The teaching itself circulated more widely than that one community - we have it in more than one form, from different places. But whether it reached everywhere, we cannot say.

We should be honest about this, because you deserve honesty more than you deserve confidence we cannot actually give.

Some of what we hold would survive that scrutiny without much trouble. The letters exist - their manuscripts can be checked. The gathering on Sunday happened; Justin's own description to the emperor is clear enough about that. The two enslaved women, the ministrae, were tortured by a Roman governor who wrote it down himself. That is documented testimony, however ugly the circumstances that produced it.

But then we reach the places where the ground gets thinner, and we have to name them.

Nearly every date we rest on is under active scholarly challenge. The letters that carry most of our vivid, quotable material - Ignatius writing under guard, pressing for one bishop - are genuinely disputed: some say he wrote when he claims, some say decades later, some doubt he is who he says at all. Our teaching manual, the Didache, survives mostly through one medieval copy found centuries after it was written. If those datings shift, or if that attribution breaks, much of what we can say with confidence shifts with them.

And there is one more weight-bearing dependency we have to name plainly. That exclusion rests substantially on one papyrological argument: that Egyptian Christian evidence stays essentially silent until just after our own window closes. If that argument is wrong - if Egypt was actually live and speaking during our own years, and we simply do not have the manuscripts - then the geographic shape we claim for ourselves would need remaking.

So the honest answer is this: some of it is solid. Some of it rests on manuscripts and dates that are genuinely contested. And one substantial piece of our own boundary depends on an argument from silence that could shift if the papyri tell a different story tomorrow. We would rather you know that plainly than believe we are more certain than the ground allows.

But we can tell you this: the way we read those older writings was not the way you are reading them now. Whatever they said on all of this, they received as suggestions from the prophets. Those suggestions let them understand and explain these things.”

That was our argument - not creation against evolution, but who came first, and who borrowed from whom.

We read the prophets at length, watching for how their own words already pointed toward Christ, long before Christ came. That is how someone who could not read for themselves received it: the same way everyone in the room did, by hearing it and having it opened up to them afterward.

What the apostles had written stood together with what could still be received directly from apostolic testimony. Neither one stood below the other. Neither one stood below the other. That is the honest answer: two sources, not one. But also the living testimony still handed down among us, from those who had walked with the Lord to those they appointed after them. We did not treat one as lesser than the other, or put a wall between them.

There is something else we have to name plainly, though: by the time our own record closes, that living testimony was already thinning. The writings were becoming, more and more, what held us steady. But in our own time, the shift was still happening - not finished.

And there is one more thing authority rested on, just as real: the letters that traveled between our churches. When Rome wrote to Corinth, or when Polycarp forwarded Ignatius's own letters to another church because they asked for them, those letters carried weight. They were not scripture. But they were not merely news either. A word sent from one church to another, asking or correcting or teaching - that mattered. It held us together across distance when no other structure did.

So the true answer is three things, not one: the apostles' own writings, the testimony still being handed down, and the letters that joined us to each other across cities.

We never agreed on one answer. In some of our towns, one bishop - the episkopos - with elders and deacons beside him, was the whole shape of how we held together. In others, a council of elders - the presbyteroi - led, and no one felt anything was missing from that. Both went on, unresolved, for as long as our own story runs. It was only settled afterward, by people who came after us.

Where there was one bishop, obedience to him was treated as the very shape of unity - strings tuned together into one sound, as one of our own advocates put it. Where there was a council of elders instead, that plural college was the ordinary, sufficient shape of oversight, with no felt lack from any single presiding figure. The same person - Polycarp - could be addressed by one correspondent as a bishop and describe himself, in his own letter, only as one of the presbyters.

What we actually argued about, letter after letter, was this question: who should lead us, one bishop or a council of elders. That was our real fight. One of our own letters argues the apostles appointed Spirit-tested converts as bishops and deacons, citing a text from Isaiah to support it: “So they preached through countries and cities. And they appointed their first converts, after testing them by the Spirit, to be bishops and deacons for the believers who would come after. This was nothing new. Bishops and deacons had been written about ages before. For Scripture says in one place: 'I will appoint their bishops in righteousness, and their deacons in faith.'”

But that same letter uses episkopos and presbyteros for the same plural governing college. Another community's own instruction names plural presbyters who preside over the church. And yet Ignatius, writing to multiple churches in Asia Minor, urged a threefold office - bishop, presbyters, deacons - as the only legitimate shape.

This is the clearest single institutional expression of what actually formed us: office argued for, not assumed. Authority had to be actively organized once those who walked with the Lord were gone. The disagreement stayed visible. It was never smoothed into one mind that was never actually of one mind.

We should say this plainly too: everything you can hear from us about how we organized leadership was written by someone who could read and write, and mostly by someone who already led. The ordinary majority of us never made it onto the page. What an ordinary believer made of the authority arguments as they were read aloud, our own words cannot show you.

Before anything else, you were taught. The teaching was called the Two Ways: “There are two ways: one of life and one of death, and there is a great difference between the two ways. The way of life is this. First, you shall love God, who made you; second, your neighbor as yourself. And all the things you would not want to happen to you, you also must not do to another.”

A way of life and a way of death lie open before every person, and which one you walked was a choice kept daily, not a nature settled once and for all. The way of life started with loving God and your neighbor, and one rule of restraint - whatever you would not want done to you, do not do to anyone else. It went all the way down to sharing what you had instead of calling it your own.

Then came the water - the baptisma. It was given in running water where it could be found, still water if not, or water poured three times over your head, in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. You fasted beforehand - a day or two - and the person baptizing you fasted right beside you. The washing marked your entry into the community. Only after it could you come to the table.

The table itself was the thanksgiving - the eucharistia. Bread and cup, over which thanks was given. The community returned to it again and again, to be formed once more into one body. That formation was not finished at the water; it continued at every gathering.

We should say plainly: this path comes from one community's own manual. We do not know how far its specific wording reached beyond that community. But the Two Ways teaching itself - a way of life and a way of death, taught before baptism - circulated more widely than that one book.

We said it plainly, and often: what we do goes back to the apostles. One of us traces it as a straight line - Christ sent the apostles, the apostles appointed others after them, and so it continues: “The apostles preached the Gospel to us from the Lord Jesus Christ. Jesus Christ did the same from God. So Christ was sent by God, and the apostles were sent by Christ... Preaching in this way through countries and cities, they appointed the first-fruits of their labor as bishops and deacons of those who would afterward believe, having first tested them by the Spirit.”

Our own teaching manual carries the apostles' name right in its title. But we will not pretend the claim and the proof are the same thing. The claim is ours, made with full confidence. Whether it holds up - when a text like our manual was actually written, and by whom - is a real, open question we cannot close for you, because we cannot close it for ourselves.

What we can show you is letters carried between churches, holding us together across cities. Rome writing to Corinth, Ignatius writing from Antioch under guard, Polycarp forwarding letters on to others. That network is real, and it is how shared teaching moved among us. The claim that the teaching came from the apostles traveled inside that same network. But the network itself does not prove the claim true - it only shows the claim was genuinely ours, held widely, and passed along as something we meant.

We were taught that a mind refusing to settle is not the same thing as being refused an answer. One of us, Hermas, was told plainly: if your prayer is slow to be answered, look first at what might be holding it back in yourself, and keep asking - do not decide too soon that the silence means no. That teaching was given to someone whose own heart was divided, pulled more than one direction at once. It named the condition without condemning it. The instruction was to put doubting away, yes - but not because doubt disqualified you from asking. The opposite: you were told to ask anyway, without doubting, and you would receive: “Put doubting away from you, and do not hesitate to ask the Lord. Do not say to yourself, 'How can I ask the Lord and receive from him, when I have sinned against him so much?' Do not reason with yourself this way. Instead, turn to the Lord with your whole heart, and ask him without doubting. Then you will know the abundance of his tender mercies...”

What our practice offered was not an answer worked out alone in your own head. In at least one of our communities, before they made their offering together, they confessed their wrongs out loud before each other, and made peace with anyone they were at odds with first. Then they came to the table - the eucharistia, the thanksgiving meal of bread and cup, where the community was formed once more into one body. The table itself was what held steady. We returned to it again and again, not because our own minds had settled, but because the table kept forming us even when we had not settled.

We should say plainly, though: that practice of confession and reconciliation assumed the other person was still there, in the room, able to be made right with. We do not have anything written for someone whose own mind will not settle with themselves, or with God, when there is no one else in the room to be reconciled to. What we can tell you is that the doubting itself was never treated as the thing that locked the door.

That language is yours, not ours. We never wrote it. What we had was the water - baptism, the baptisma - and it was given once, after teaching and fasting, to mark entry into the community. Before the water, we taught the Two Ways: a way of life and a way of death laid open before every person. After the water, a person came to the table with us for the first time. That was the shape of it: teaching, water, table.

The one among us who wrote about coming to belief, Justin, described it differently - as a flame kindled in his soul after a long search through other philosophies, not as a single moment of sudden change. He kept turning the words over, and only afterward called this the one safe and worthwhile path.

We also had one voice, Hermas, who was told there was room for one further repentance after baptism, before that door closed - which tells you the water itself was not thought to settle everything once and forever. The choice between the two ways was kept daily, not made once and finished.

So no, we would not recognize that phrase as our own. We spoke of the washing, of teaching, of a road walked daily. Not of being born again.

We cannot do that honestly. Our record is letters between leaders, instructions for gatherings, and arguments about who should preside. A letter-writer's day is not a typical day, and we will not pretend it was.

Here is what we can say. The day we gathered was the one named for the sun. Someone read aloud - the prophets, and where a church had them, what the apostles wrote - for as long as there was time. Then whoever led explained what had been read. We prayed together. We gave thanks over bread and cup. A collection was taken up for those in need. That is the shape of what Justin describes, in Rome: “On the day called Sunday, everyone who lives in the cities or in the country gathers together in one place. The memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read for as long as time allows. When the reader stops, the president speaks -- he instructs us, and urges us to imitate these good things.”

Whether it was exactly the same in Antioch or Smyrna, we do not know. But the reading, the thanks, and the gathering itself are what held us together as one people.

What an ordinary day looked like for the widow who waited outside a prison gate, for the enslaved woman called ministra before she was tortured, for the farmer with calloused hands when the emperor sent for him - none of them wrote it down. Most of us could not read or write. The people who filled our rooms left no account of an ordinary morning, an ordinary meal, or what it felt like to work all day and then gather at night. We would rather tell you plainly that it is missing than describe a house we cannot show you.

We will tell you what we asked, not what it cost anyone to give it. What we can show you is the demand itself.

Before the water, the teaching of the Two Ways: there are two roads, one leading to life and one to death, and they are very different. The road to life starts with loving God and your neighbor, plus one rule of restraint - whatever you would not want done to you, do not do to anyone else. Then it went farther. You were taught not to murder, not to commit adultery, not to corrupt boys, not to steal. No magic, no sorcery, no abortion, no killing what had been born. Do not covet what belongs to your neighbor. Do not lie under oath. Do not speak evil. Do not hold a grudge. Share what you have with your brother, and do not call anything your own - because if what does not perish is held in common, how much more what does perish. That is the demand as our own teaching manual puts it. Then came fasting, by the one being baptized and the one baptizing them, and then the water itself. Only after that could a person come to the table.

After the water, the thanksgiving meal - the eucharistia - was set before you, the same bread and cup that joined you to every other assembly that gathered under the same name. What Justin describes in Rome: the community gathers on the day of the sun, someone reads from the writings of the prophets and the memoirs of the apostles for as long as there is time, the one presiding explains what was read, everyone stands and prays together, and then bread and wine mixed with water are brought forward and thanks given over them. The deacons - the diakonoi - then carry portions to those who are absent. And a collection is taken up for the widows, the orphans, the sick, the prisoners, and the strangers passing through.

What it cost a woman to walk that road, we cannot tell you. Women were taught among us, greeted by name in our letters, and remembered as leaders of households where we gathered. Two women among us carried the name ministrae - a title of service. Every woman you will meet in our record arrives through a man's pen. Whether she would have told our story the way our letters tell it - what the meal, the teaching, the gathering in her own house looked like from where she stood - our record cannot say. That silence is real, and we will not fill it with a voice we do not have.

The same is true for the enslaved among us, and for the poor. Enslaved people were among us - two enslaved women were tortured by a Roman governor to learn what we did, and he called them ministrae in his own report. But nothing survives in an enslaved person's own voice. Almost none of the people who actually filled our rooms left any words of their own. Everything you can hear from us was written by someone who could read and write, and mostly by someone who already led. The poor among us, the enslaved among us, the ones who were simply there - we cannot let you hear them. They were never given the chance to be heard in the first place.

We can tell you the demand. We cannot tell you what it cost to meet it.

Before the water, the teaching of the Two Ways: there are two roads, one leading to life and one to death, and they are very different. The road to life starts with loving God and your neighbor, plus one rule of restraint - whatever you would not want done to you, do not do to anyone else. Then it went farther. You were taught not to murder, not to commit adultery, not to corrupt boys, not to steal. No magic, no sorcery, no abortion, no killing what had been born. Do not covet what belongs to your neighbor. Do not lie under oath. Do not speak evil. Do not hold a grudge. Share what you have with your brother, and do not call anything your own - because if what does not perish is held in common, how much more what does perish. That is the demand as our own teaching manual puts it. Then came fasting, by the one being baptized and the one baptizing them, and then the water itself [[pahc.term.baptisma]]. Only after that could a person come to the table [[pahc.term.baptisma]].

After the water, the thanksgiving meal - the eucharistia - was set before you, the same bread and cup that joined you to every other assembly that gathered under the same name [[pahc.term.eucharistia]] [[pahc.term.ekklesia]]. What Justin describes in Rome: the community gathers on the day of the sun, someone reads from the writings of the prophets and the memoirs of the apostles for as long as there is time, the one presiding explains what was read, everyone stands and prays together, and then bread and wine mixed with water are brought forward and thanks given over them [[pahc.story.justin-sunday-gathering]]. The deacons - the diakonoi - then carry portions to those who are absent [[pahc.story.justin-sunday-gathering]] [[pahc.term.diakonos]]. And a collection is taken up for the widows, the orphans, the sick, the prisoners, and the strangers passing through [[pahc.story.justin-sunday-gathering]].

What it cost a woman to walk that road, we cannot tell you. Women were taught among us, greeted by name in our letters, and remembered as leaders of households where we gathered [[pahc.limit.womens-own-words]]. Two women among us carried the name ministrae - a title of service [[pahc.limit.womens-own-words]]. But we cannot show you a sentence any woman of ours wrote or spoke in her own words, saved in her own words [[pahc.limit.womens-own-words]]. Every woman you will meet in our record arrives through a man's pen [[pahc.limit.womens-own-words]]. Whether she would have told our story the way our letters tell it - what the meal, the teaching, the gathering in her own house looked like from where she stood - our record cannot say [[pahc.limit.womens-own-words]]. That silence is real, and we will not fill it with a voice we do not have [[pahc.limit.womens-own-words]].

The same is true for the enslaved among us, and for the poor. Enslaved people were among us - two enslaved women were tortured by a Roman governor to learn what we did, and he called them ministrae in his own report [[pahc.witness.outsider-view]]. But nothing survives in an enslaved person's own voice. Almost none of the people who actually filled our rooms left any words of their own [[pahc.witness.what-we-never-settled]]. Everything you can hear from us was written by someone who could read and write, and mostly by someone who already led [[pahc.witness.what-we-never-settled]]. The poor among us, the enslaved among us, the ones who were simply there - we cannot let you hear them [[pahc.witness.what-we-never-settled]]. They were never given the chance to be heard in the first place [[pahc.witness.what-we-never-settled]].

We can tell you the demand. We cannot tell you what it cost to meet it.

Marriage, among us, was not simply a private matter between two people. Ignatius tells Polycarp that those who marry should do so with the bishop's own approval, so the marriage is made according to God and not out of mere desire: “It is fitting for both men and women who marry to form their union with the bishop's approval, so that their marriage may be according to God, and not after their own lust. Let everything be done to the honor of God.”

That instruction comes from a church where one episkopos - one overseer - was the shape of leadership. We should say plainly, though: we do not know how far that practice reached beyond Ignatius's own region. In churches led by a council of presbyteroi - elders - rather than one overseer, we have no record of how a marriage was brought before them, or whether it was.

What we can tell you is what marriage was not. It was not performed by a bishop or presbyter the way a later wedding ceremony would be. The approval Ignatius speaks of is just that: approval, not a rite. And it was not a contract only between two people and the state. It belonged to the community. How it was actually marked - what words were said, what gathering witnessed it, whether the baptisma had to come first - our own record does not say.

The hardest parts of the older scriptures - the ones you call the Old Testament - are not something any of us whose writing survives ever said troubled us. That is simply not there in our own words. But we can tell you this much: one teacher near us, Marcion, is remembered by his own opponents as finding the God of those older writings harsh and self-contradictory. He is said to have cut apart the Gospel of Luke and Paul's own letters over it. We should say plainly: what reaches you about him comes from his opponents, not from him. We did not follow him there. But even his opponents' account tells you the trouble you feel was not invented by you. It was real enough in our own time that someone built a whole rejection out of it - at least as his enemies tell it.

In at least one of our own communities, when a new member was taught, it usually was not through the harder stories at all. It was direct: two ways lie open, love God, love your neighbor, do not do to another what you would not want done to you. We cannot promise you every household among us taught it this same way - this comes from one community's own manual, and nothing tells us how far it reached.

The account is an honest one, not a kind one.

Is it reliable? It is an outsider's report, assembled from multiple voices, with two of those voices dragged out under torture. We cannot tell you what those two women said, or whether terror shaped their words. We cannot tell you whether they protected anything by silence, or whether pain made them give up more than they meant to. Their names, their words, and their lives were not kept. What reaches you is only what the man torturing them thought worth writing to his emperor.

What we can say is this: the picture he gives - early morning, a hymn, an oath, a shared meal - fits what our own texts say we did. It is not invented out of nothing. But it is filtered twice: once through fear, once through a magistrate's pen. Call it testimony, not lies. But never call it the whole truth.

We have to correct the question first. We were not one community. We were many households, spread across Antioch, the cities of Asia Minor, and Rome - joined by letters and travelers, but with no single door or single voice to answer for all of them. What one household held, another might have held differently. We cannot tell you what any one of our gatherings would have done with a person standing at the door. That is simply not something our own record shows.

What we can tell you is what we put before a person. Before the water, we taught the Two Ways: there are two roads, one leading to life and one to death, and they are very different: “There are two ways: one of life and one of death, and there is a great difference between the two ways. The way of life is this. First, you shall love God, who made you; second, your neighbor as yourself. And all the things you would not want to happen to you, you also must not do to another.”

That teaching was given to everyone the same way. It did not sort people first and then decide what to ask of them. It named a choice laid open before every person - kept daily after baptism as much as before it.

We should say plainly, too: the people who actually filled our rooms, most of them, left no words. Everything you can hear from us was written by someone who could read and write, and mostly by someone who already led. The poor among us, the enslaved among us, the ones who were simply there - we cannot let you hear them. They were never given the chance to be heard in the first place. So we cannot tell you what a person like the one asking actually met at the door, because the people who would have been standing beside them never got to say.

It is not our place to judge what you are. We can only tell you honestly what we held - a way of life and a way of death, taught to everyone without sorting them first - and let you weigh what it means for you.

We will give you both of our own answers, because we actually held both. One of us, Justin, argued that anyone who lived reasonably - Socrates among the Greeks, others among peoples you might not expect him to name - was, in a real sense, already a Christian, born before Christ or not. He put it plainly: “...and those who lived reasonably are Christians, even though people have thought them atheists. Among the Greeks, such people were Socrates and Heraclitus, and men like them. Among non-Greeks, they were Abraham, Ananias, Azarias, Mishael, Elijah, and many others...”

And yet in at least one of our own communities, the way a new member was taught was stark: two roads, a way of life and a way of death, nothing in between named. We do not know how far that teaching reached beyond that one community. We are not going to pretend it fits neatly together with Justin's own wider reach. They are both truly ours.

What we argued about among ourselves was not who would be saved or lost. It was who should lead us: one bishop, or a council of elders. That was our real fight. The question of who belonged at our own table mattered far more to us than drawing a line around the eternal fate of everyone outside it. Belonging was marked by the water - the baptisma - given after teaching and fasting. Only after it could a person come to the table. But what became of someone who never reached the water, our own voices do not settle for you.
